## 1. DIGITAL ADOPTION AND E-COMMERCE

### 1.1 Internet and Device Usage Among Seniors

According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' (MIC) 2023 Communications Usage Trend Survey, 93% of people in their 60s and 81% of those in their 70s use digital devices [6]. However, internet usage drops to just 13% for those 80+ [6]. MIC's 2023 Communications Usage Trend Survey also reports that 90.2% of people in their 60s and 67% of those in their 70s are online, with smartphone ownership at 93% and 81%, respectively, dispelling the myth that seniors are offline [7].

By 2022 in China (for comparison context), 153 million seniors (54.5%) were online, with screen time reaching 127.2 hours per month by 2023 [4].

### 1.2 Generational Differences: "Younger Old" vs. "Older Old"

The 2023 Communications Usage Survey shows a stark drop-off after age 80: 93% of 60-somethings and 81% of 70-somethings use digital devices, but internet usage drops to just 13% for those 80+ [6]. This confirms a significant generational divide between the "younger old" (65-74) and "older old" (75+), with the 80+ group being almost entirely offline.

### 1.3 E-Commerce Adoption and Online Shopping

Japan's total e-commerce volume for 2024 is US$380 billion, with retail e-commerce at US$121 billion. The CAGR for 2024–2027 is 7%, with a forecasted market size of US$465 billion by 2027. 98% of Japan's population is banked. 95% of e-commerce sales are domestic, and 76% of the population (94 million people) shop online. Japanese consumers spend up to US$455 per single product, well above the global average of US$378 [10].

Online shopping growth accelerated by 4 to 6 years during the COVID-19 pandemic, with a 77% year-over-year sales increase. Seniors 65+ became the fastest-growing group of online shoppers with a 49% increase in sales. 86% of people over 61 are expected to transition to online shopping. Instacart sign-ups for shoppers 60+ tripled, and they order groceries 25% more frequently and spend 35% more on household items than average [9].

A study showed that only 55.3% of seniors were able to complete tasks on ecommerce websites (as opposed to 75% among a younger audience). Seniors are 20% more likely to use BOPIS (Buy Online, Pick Up in Store) [9].

Payment methods in Japan by volume: Credit cards (63%), Digital wallets (15%), Cash (8%), Other (8%), BNPL (3%), Bank transfers (2%), Debit cards (1%). Device usage: Mobile (56%), Desktop (44%) [10].

Top-selling categories (2023): Food, beverages & alcohol (US$21B), Electrical & electronic products (US$20B), Clothing & accessories (US$20B), Household goods & furniture (US$18B), Books & audiovisual software (US$14B) [10].

Top online stores by traffic: Amazon (35%), Rakuten (32%), Mercari (7%), DMM.com (6%), MonotaRO (2%) [10].

Over 25% of Thrive Market's consumer base is now older than 65 after implementing senior-friendly features [9].

### 1.4 E-Commerce Adaptations for Seniors

Usability improvements include Fujitsu's "Rakuraku" series (large buttons, voice guidance) and Amazon's Senior Mode (larger search bars, AI warnings against accidental orders) [6]. Payment and delivery adaptations include cash-on-delivery, convenience store payments, scheduled delivery, and concierge services [6]. High-growth categories include health/wellness products (supplements, home medical devices), online supermarkets (Aeon), and meal delivery services (Oisix, Watami) [6]. Fraud prevention measures include AI anomaly detection, family-linked order approval notifications, and Consumer Affairs Agency interface guidelines [6]. Future trends include health management apps linked with e-commerce, collaboration with local governments, and seniors running their own online shops on C2C platforms like Rakuma and BASE [6].

### 1.5 Problems and Risks for Elderly Online Shoppers

Consultations related to online shopping by people aged 60+ reached 25,800 in fiscal 2019 at the National Consumer Affairs Center, a 15-fold increase from 2010, far outpacing the under-59 group (less than 6 times). Health food online orders by seniors surged 102 times. The elderly are estimated to have three times the rate of online shopping problems as younger people [8].

Key causes include unfamiliarity with online interfaces, small confirmation warnings, and cognitive decline/dementia. An 86-year-old with dementia spent 10 million yen ($94,800) in six months repeatedly buying the same products. Many Alzheimer's patients repeatedly purchase the same product. E-commerce sites with screen designs that guide purchases can be dangerous for dementia patients with impaired judgment, said Jin Narumoto, a professor at Kyoto Prefectural University of Medicine [8].

Nikkei tested major e-commerce platforms by ordering the same product repeatedly. Amazon showed duplicate purchase warnings at the top of the screen, but Rakuten and Yahoo lacked such warnings during ordering. Experts note that warning placement is often poor for seniors, font sizes are too small, and dementia patients can only process up to six objects on screen at once [8].

With nearly 7 million elderly single-person households in Japan and increasing internet usage due to COVID-19, the article calls for better anomaly detection systems using big data to protect elderly online shoppers, noting that most e-commerce platforms lack adequate safeguards [8].

"It would be hard to make the case that it's illegal, because the regulations aren't in place," said Takaaki Someya, a lawyer who specializes in e-commerce. "But as a matter of corporate ethics, there needs to be kind of mechanism to handle it" [8].

---

## 2. HEALTH-CONSCIOUS FOOD CHOICES

### 2.1 Functional Foods Market Size

The Japan functional food market reached USD 14.60 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 24.50 billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 5.93% during 2026-2034 [11].

The Japan health and wellness foods market was valued at USD 25.40 billion in 2025, projected to reach USD 26.59 billion in 2026 and USD 42.10 billion by 2036, growing at a CAGR of 4.7% (2026–2036), representing an incremental opportunity of USD 15.51 billion. Functional Foods lead with 44% share in 2026 by product type. Offline dominates with 79% share in 2026 (drugstores, supermarkets, convenience stores); online is growing among younger demographics [14].

The Japan Health and Wellness Market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 3.96% from 2024 to 2032, with functional foods as a significant contributor [13].

### 2.2 Foods with Function Claims (FFC) System

The FFC system (introduced in 2015) uses a notification-based approach, leading to rapid market expansion from JPY 31 billion to JPY 357 billion by 2020, surpassing the FOSHU market size of JPY 321 billion in the same year [15].

Japan's multi-tiered regulatory system includes Foods with Specified Health Uses (FOSHU), Foods with Nutrient Function Claims (FNFC), and Foods with Function Claims (FFC), plus unregulated "so-called health foods" [15].

The FFC system administered by the Consumer Affairs Agency has created a regulatory pathway that rewards evidence-based product positioning over generic wellness branding. Manufacturers relying on unsubstantiated health marketing without functional claim registrations will face declining shelf allocation [14].

The Beni-koji (red yeast rice) contamination incident in 2024 highlighted regulatory adjustments needed in the risk-benefit balance [15].

### 2.3 Consumer Behavior and Demographics

The market is driven by rising health consciousness, an aging population seeking preventive care, and government-backed FFC/FOSHU certifications enabling science-based health claims [11].

A study of 392 Japanese adults found that 31% used fortified foods/supplements, with up to 20.6% of vitamin B6 intake coming from supplemental sources [11].

Japanese consumers value efficiency and trustworthiness in products, with high expectations for detail and quality [13].

For the aging population, functional foods that help prevent the deterioration of joints, bones, and muscles are ideal [13].

Functional foods and drinks in Japan are also known for their benefits in balancing gut bacteria, managing weight, combating stressful lifestyles, and supporting specific beauty goals, such as maintaining clear and supple skin [13].

Popular functional foods target gut health (probiotic lactobacilli, oligosaccharides, dietary fiber in yogurts), cholesterol/triglyceride reduction, blood pressure and blood sugar control, oral care, and stress relief [13].

### 2.4 Product Innovations and Key Players

On July 26, 2024, Meiji launched functional chocolates sweetened with FOS (fructooligosaccharides) - low-calorie, gut-friendly chocolates registered under Foods with Function Claims by Japan's Consumer Affairs Agency [11].

Nestlé S.A. holds the largest share at 29.5%, offering a broad range of nutritional products including protein-fortified items, dietary foods, and functional beverages that appeal to both aging consumers and health-conscious younger buyers [14].

Key players include Danone S.A., PepsiCo Inc., General Mills Inc., and Kraft Heinz Company [14].

### 2.5 Regional Growth in Health and Wellness Foods (CAGR 2026–2036)

| Region | CAGR |
|---|---|
| Kyushu & Okinawa | 5.9% |
| Kanto | 5.4% |
| Kansai | 4.8% |
| Chubu | 4.2% |
| Tohoku | 3.7% |
| Rest of Japan | 3.5% |

### 2.6 Statista Data Points

Health foods market shipment value in Japan (FY 2016-2025) tracked in billion Japanese yen. Functional foods (foods with function claims) market size (FY 2015-2026) with forecasts. Production value of health foods in Japan (2016-2024) in billion U.S. dollars. Nutrition market size in Japan (FY 2021-2030) in trillion Japanese yen. Health and functional food ingredient market size (FY 2022-2025) in billion Japanese yen. Health food OEM (contract manufacturing) market size (FY 2016-2023) in billion Japanese yen. Drugstores health food sales revenue in Japan (2014-2023) in billion Japanese yen. Dietary supplements market size in Japan (2019-2026) in billion Japanese yen. Number of new registrations for foods with function claims (FY 2015-2024). Total number of health foods with function claims registered as of July 2026, by application and by ingredient. Awareness of foods with health claims in Japan (March 2024). Share of consumers who have tried FOSHU health foods and foods with function claims (March 2024). Preferred purchase channels for dietary and health supplements in Japan (February 2024). Level of trust in functional foods claims in Japan (April 2024). Frequency of consuming functional foods and dietary supplements (April 2024). Leading supplement ingredients consumed in Japan (December 2024) [12].

---

## 3. AGING-IN-PLACE AND HOUSING MODIFICATIONS

### 3.1 Home Renovation Market

The Japan home renovation market in 2023 was estimated at ¥7.3575 trillion, reflecting 0.6% year-on-year growth. Major renovations exceeding 10 square meters grew by 5.2%, driven by rising construction material costs and labor shortages. However, demand for smaller-scale renovations and furniture-related improvements declined as consumer behavior shifted following COVID-19's reclassification as a Class 5 disease. The market is projected to shrink by 3.2% in 2024 to ¥7.1 trillion, and further decline to ¥7 trillion in 2025, due to reduced consumer home improvement demand post-pandemic, though per-project costs are expected to remain elevated [17].

The Japan home improvement market is valued at approximately USD 25 billion and is growing due to urbanization, rising incomes, DIY trends, and demand for energy-efficient and smart home upgrades. The 35–54 years age group dominates the market. Leading participants include LIXIL Corporation, Takara Standard Co., Ltd., Panasonic Holdings Corporation, Daikin Industries, Ltd., TOTO Ltd., Asahi Kasei Corporation, Misawa Homes Co., Ltd., Sekisui House, Ltd., Sumitomo Forestry Co., Ltd., Nitori Holdings Co., Ltd., YKK AP Inc., KMEW Co., Ltd., Kohnan Shoji Co., Ltd., Marubeni Corporation, Sanei Co., Ltd. [19].

### 3.2 Barrier-Free Improvements and Senior Housing Demand

Age-appropriate housing renovations grew 23% in 2022, with over 780,000 residences receiving barrier-free improvements [18].

The "Japan 2025 Problem" refers to the year when all members of Japan's post-war baby boomer generation (born 1947–1949) will be aged 75 or older, with over 18% of the population becoming "late-stage elderly." This shift is significantly reshaping Japan's real estate market. Key market impacts include: a surge in vacant homes (akiya), especially in rural and suburban areas; declining demand for traditional family homes; rising demand for senior-friendly, barrier-free housing near healthcare in urban centers like Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya; and an urban-rural market divergence where Tokyo's residential prices rose over 10% year-on-year in early 2025 [16].

Investment opportunities identified include: akiya renovation and repurposing (supported by government subsidies), senior housing development in metropolitan areas, and urban redevelopment projects. Challenges include labor shortages in construction and property management and fragmented market conditions requiring careful location selection [16].

### 3.3 Residential Construction Market

The Japan Residential Construction Market size was valued at USD 262 Billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 401 Billion by 2032, growing at a CAGR of 5.4% from 2026 to 2032. Government housing subsidies and tax incentives totaled ¥465 billion in FY2022. The "Flat 35" loan program has supported nearly 1.2 million new house purchases. 29.1% of Japan's population is over 65, with a projected increase to 35.3% by 2040. Over 13% of existing dwellings (5.3 million units) require seismic retrofitting. Seismic retrofit spending totaled ¥289 billion in FY2022 [18].

Tokyo contributes around 27% of Japan's overall residential construction value, with new housing starts reaching 153,000 units by 2022. Osaka is seeing impressive growth in residential buildings, with a 24% year-over-year rise in new home starts in 2022, reaching 82,000 units [18].

### 3.4 Smart Care Buildings and Nursing Home Design Standards

An academic article published in *Frontiers in Public Health* (2025) proposes revisions to Japan's nursing home design standards and regulations by integrating smart devices to address the challenges of a super-aging society. The study follows a three-phase methodology: (1) reviewing existing Japanese regulations (e.g., Older Population Welfare Act, Barrier-Free Law) and identifying current coverage in daily care, mobility safety, and privacy; (2) projecting next-generation older population housing needs based on a 2018 nationwide survey (879 respondents aged 20-39 as proxies for 2050 seniors), yielding six demand categories—Family Care, Daily Care, Safe Mobility, Privacy, Daily Recreation, and Achieving Value—and selecting smart devices categorized into three functional types (sensors, data transmission devices, and accessibility/operability devices); and (3) proposing regulatory improvements, including reclassifying four of six core welfare services (condition monitoring, lifestyle counseling, household services, and health maintenance) as "smart services" enabled by IoT, AI, and remote monitoring technologies. Key findings indicate that smart devices can reduce caregiver workload, enable real-time health tracking, improve emergency alerts, and alleviate staffing shortages in nursing homes [20].

Currently available smart medical and assistive devices on the market can be broadly categorized into three functional types based on ISO 9999:2022 and ISO/IEC 30141:2018: (1) Sensors that detect human movement, (2) Devices that transmission and sharing of user information, and (3) Devices that enhance operability and accessibility [20].

---

## 4. TRANSPORTATION PATTERNS

### 4.1 License Surrender (運転免許返納) Trends

In 2017, 423,800 elderly people returned their driver's licenses, marking the highest number since the system was introduced in 1998. 253,900 people aged 75 or older returned their licenses, which was a 56% increase over the previous year. Despite the increase in the elderly forgoing driving, there were still 5.4 million drivers aged 75 or older in Japan as of the end of 2017, so that the proportion returning their licenses is only around 5% [21].

Drivers 75+ must renew licenses every three years and undergo cognitive testing; those at risk for dementia must consult a doctor. Municipalities offer incentives like public transit discounts, but giving up driving is difficult in mountainous areas with limited public transportation, requiring complementary measures to address mobility needs [21].

### 4.2 Accident Rates and Safety Concerns

In 2018, drivers 75 or older caused 14.8% of fatal accidents (up from 8.7% in 2008), and over-75s caused 8.2 fatal crashes per 100,000 drivers — about 2.4 times the rate of younger drivers. However, drivers aged 16-19 remain the most dangerous group (11.1 fatal accidents per 100,000) [23].

Japan currently requires over-75s to take cognitive tests every three years for license renewal, and proposals have been made to restrict elderly drivers to cars with automatic braking systems. Over 400,000 elderly Japanese voluntarily surrendered their licenses in 2017 [23].

### 4.3 The Process of License Surrender (Qualitative Study)

A qualitative study published in Sage Open Aging on July 1, 2025 (PMCID: PMC12219472) explored the driving cessation process among older adults in urban Japan using the Trajectory Equifinality Model (TEM). Semi-structured interviews were conducted with four participants (aged 75–82, mean 77.3 years) who had surrendered their driver's license within the past 3 years. Four phases were identified: (1) Driving Continuation Phase - balancing risks to society and personal convenience; (2) Driving Cessation Preparation Phase - embracing the challenge of a life without driving; (3) Lifestyle Confidence Phase - establishing a life independent of driving and licensing; (4) License Surrender Decision Phase - resolving to relinquish the driver's license [24].

A key finding was the distinction between practical driving cessation and formal license surrender, which do not always coincide. Participants continued to hold licenses even after stopping driving, with the license renewal deadline serving as a decisive moment for formal surrender. Participants experienced minimal distress and gradually transitioned out of driving in a self-determined manner, attributed to urban-specific characteristics like availability of alternative transportation [24].

### 4.4 Substitution of Driving with Public Transport and Online Services

A peer-reviewed article published in Travel Behaviour and Society (Volume 43, April 2026) examined how people in Shiga prefecture, Japan, might substitute in-person mobility with online services for daily necessities if their driver's licenses were revoked. The study used a stated-choice survey of 645 individuals and found that older adults are generally willing to shift from car use to public transport rather than forgo travel entirely when driving is no longer an option. Substitution of in-person mobility with online alternatives is higher among individuals who are tech-savvy, socially supported, or have access to cars. In-person activities are less replaceable for older adults, likely due to the sensory nature of shopping and the relational quality of social interaction that online formats cannot replicate [25].

### 4.5 Urban Environment and Health Outcomes

A 2025 study analyzed the relationship between changes in health status and the urban/transportation environment among elderly Japanese individuals who have returned their driver's licenses. Using panel survey data from 2022 and 2023 in Funabashi City, Chiba Prefecture, the study examined 180 respondents aged 65+ who had returned their licenses. The results showed that the more facilities around the home, such as supermarkets, the less the decline in activity capacity [22].

### 4.6 Autonomous Vehicles and Future Solutions

Solutions being explored include self-driving taxis (road tests began in 2016), 'limited driver's licenses' for cars with safety supports, Toyota's tiny two-seater electric car for short drives, and continued driver education and occupational therapy [23].

"You can't say at X point in someone's chronological age, they are likely to experience specific declines," says Alana Officer, a disability and rehabilitation coordinator at the WHO. "It's important to take steps that support public safety, while treating older drivers with dignity," says Toshiko Kaneda, senior research associate at Population Reference Bureau. "Many people easily discuss that elderly drivers should return their driver's licence – but we shouldn't forget about those people's feelings," says Tomomi Makino, a Toyota quality advisor. "Without a car, they cannot survive. They cannot go shopping or see their friends and so on. To enjoy life, a car is necessary," says Hidenori Arai, president of Japan's National Center for Geriatrics and Gerontology. "If you build people's cognitive capacity, it has great promise to extend to safe driving," says WHO's Alana Officer [23].

---

## 5. SINGLE-ELDERLY HOUSEHOLDS

### 5.1 Demographic Data

As of June 2023, Japan had 54,452,000 households, with single-person households making up 34.0% (18,495,000) — the highest proportion since 2019. The average household size is declining to 2.23 people [26].

49.5% of households (26,951,000) include elderly people aged 65+. Among these, 32.0% are married couples only, 31.7% are single-person households, and 20.2% are parents with unmarried children. Among elderly single-person households, 64.4% are women. The largest age group for men is 70-74 (27.7%), while for women it's 85+ (24.9%) [26].

Only 18.1% of households (9,835,000) have children under 18 — the second consecutive year below 10 million. Among these, 48.6% have one child, 39.7% have two, and 11.7% have three or more. Average children per household is 1.65 [26].

Projections by the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research show single-person households reaching 44.3% by 2050. The proportion of unmarried individuals in single-person elderly households is projected to rise sharply: from 33.7% (men) and 11.94% (women) in 2020 to 59.7% (men) and 30.2% (women) in 2050, suggesting a future increase in elderly people with no close relatives [26].

### 5.2 Consumption Patterns of Single-Elderly Households

The per capita energy consumption of single-elderly households is larger than that of households composed of parents and children by 82.9% [29].

Single households present higher carbon footprints than non-single households, with those of single females surpassing their male counterparts due to increased household energy use and expenditures on clothing and healthcare. By 2040, single households are expected to account for approximately 31.1% of Japan's emissions from households, challenging national decarbonization efforts due to their higher per capita emissions [30].

Housing energy and food consumption remain the dominant carbon footprint contributors across all demographic sectors [30].

The number of households headed by people aged 70 and older with total annual incomes less than ¥2 million have grown 1.4 times to 450,000 from 320,000 five years ago and 2.2 times from 200,000 ten years ago [28].

### 5.3 Generational Differences in Household Structure

Currently, single-person households are often formed due to the death of a spouse or the spouse entering a care facility, but in the future, a sharp increase in the number of elderly people with no close relatives at all is expected [26].

### 5.4 Household Energy Consumption Effects

A study examining how population aging affects household energy consumption using micro-level data from 1989 to 2014 assessed three effects: the pure aging effect (elderly people stay home more and require more heating/cooling), the cohort effect (different generations have different lifestyle-based energy use patterns), and the family structure effect (household size shrinkage leads to diseconomies of scale). Japan's elderly population (65+) rose from 12.9% in 1990 to 30.7% in 2010 [29].

Key findings: Pure aging effect - Household energy consumption increased by about 12% from 1995 to 2015 due to aging. Seniors over 75 use 50% more energy than those in their early 20s. Family structure effect - Due to shrinking household size, energy consumption increased by about 16.6% from 1990 to 2015. Cohort effect - Younger generations consume less energy than older generations. The cohort born 1975-1980 uses 16.7% less energy than those born 1950-1954, likely due to living in smaller houses and more energy-efficient lifestyles, but this only partially offsets the increase from aging effects [29].

Per capita energy consumption shows a U-shaped relationship to age, decreasing in the 20s, minimizing in the 30s, and increasing after that [29].

---

## 6. PENSION ADEQUACY AND WILLINGNESS TO SPEND

### 6.1 Elderly Household Income and Consumption

Senior consumption, defined as the consumption of households where the head of the household is aged 60 or older, was estimated at ¥115 trillion in 2014. This is 48% of overall personal consumption and corresponds to 24% of nominal GDP. The consumption expenditures of households of people aged 60 and older have grown by an annual average of 3.1% between 2003 and 2014, while consumption by households under 60 declined by 1.9% annually over the same period. On a per-household basis, younger households still spend more (¥275,000/month) than elderly households (¥230,000/month) [28].

54% of people aged 70 and older have annual incomes less than ¥2 million, a figure that has grown 2.2 times over ten years, highlighting concerns about old-age insolvency as pension benefits fall short [28].

Food is the largest consumption expenditure for the elderly, with preferences for fresh fish, vegetables, and fruits over eating out. Elderly households have high medical care expenses and social expenses (gifts, dining out), but lower spending on housing, clothing, and transportation [28].

The latest Family Income & Expenditure Survey data show that non-working elderly households spend an average of ¥254,453 per month, up 1.1% in nominal terms year-on-year, making them a lucrative business target [7].

### 6.2 Per Capita vs. Per Household Analysis

On average, under-60 households have 2.55 persons per household, whereas senior households have just 1.87. As a result, seniors actually spend about 7% more per person. Seniors spend much more than younger households on inviting friends over for dinner, about the same on culture and recreation, and far less on educational expenses. Overall, consumption per capita fell only 1.3% from 2012-2022. The bottom line: aging is not the cause of falling consumption. Part is due to an almost 2% decline in the number of people since 2013 and part is due to stagnant and/or falling income [36].

### 6.3 Elderly as a Share of Consumption

Today, 35% of the Japanese population is older than 60, while their share of the consumption market is about half. These older households are net savers, so higher rates benefit their balance sheets, and stable pension gains further support their spending. Households in their 30s and 40s tend to be net debtors due to large mortgage balances that are overwhelmingly floating rate loans, making them vulnerable to higher rates [38].

### 6.4 Household Spending Trends

Japan's household spending dropped 3.3% year-on-year in June 2026, deepening from a 0.4% decline in the prior month and defying market expectations for a 1.0% rise. This marks the seventh consecutive month of contraction and the sharpest drop in the sequence, highlighting persistent weakness in consumer demand. Spending declined across food (-2.5%), utilities (-7.1%), furniture (-11.4%), clothing (-19.9%), and transport (-5.7%). On a seasonally adjusted monthly basis, household spending dropped 6.4%, reversing May's 3.7% gain and marking the steepest monthly fall since January 2021 [37].

### 6.5 Social Security and Healthcare Costs

Japan's FY2023 social security benefits totaled ¥135.5 trillion (22.76% of GDP, ¥1.089 million per capita). The breakdown: pensions ¥56.4T (41.6%), healthcare ¥45.6T (33.6%), and welfare/other ¥33.5T (24.7%). Long-term care expenditure (¥11.5T) has grown 2.6x since 2001. Japan's social expenditure-to-GDP ratio of 23.5% exceeds the OECD average (~21%) but is below France (~31%) and Sweden (~26%) [34].

The system shows severe intergenerational asymmetry: those 60+ receive approximately ¥65M more in lifetime benefits than they contribute, while future generations face a net burden of ~¥52M. The benefit-to-contribution ratio for those born in 1940 is 2.3x, but drops to 0.6x for those born in the 2000s. All working-age cohorts (20s-50s) are in net burden positions [34].

Healthcare costs are driven by aging (75+ per capita costs are 4x those under 65), advancing medical technology, rising pharmaceutical costs, and lifestyle disease prevalence. Long-term care premiums have tripled from 0.6% to 1.82% in 23 years. The FY2025 social security budget of ¥38.3T accounts for 56% of general government expenditure, severely constraining fiscal flexibility. Long-term care expenditure is projected to reach ~¥25.8T by FY2040, more than double current levels [34].

### 6.6 Pension System Status

Japan's public pension reserves have climbed above the ¥300 trillion mark for the first time, reaching a record ¥302.5893 trillion at the end of fiscal 2025. National Pension: ¥70.9 billion surplus. Employees' Pension Insurance: ¥1.7653 trillion surplus. The milestone comes as Japan faces a profound demographic challenge, with a rapidly ageing population and a shrinking working-age population [32].

Japan has over 130 million people, and more than 30% of these people are more than 65 years old; furthermore, it was forecasted that by 2065, 38% of the Japanese population would be over 65 years of age. The old-age dependency ratio is anticipated to attain 73.2 by 2050, indicating nearly one retiree for each working-age individual. By 2040, Japan's pension expenditures are projected to exceed 30% of GDP [33].

### 6.7 Gender Pension Gap

Women receive monthly pensions that are about one-quarter lower than men's on average across OECD countries, ranging from less than 10% lower in Czechia, Estonia, Iceland, the Slovak Republic and Slovenia to more than 35% lower in Austria, Mexico, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, and reaching 47% lower in Japan [39].

Gender differences in employment, hours worked and hourly wages make a similar contribution to the gender gap in lifetime earnings (about one-third each), which averages 35% across OECD countries [39].

### 6.8 Pension Savings and Returns Gap

Over three-fourths of respondents were 'concerned for post-retirement life,' with respondents in their thirties and forties being highly concerned (85% and 83%, respectively). Only about 10% of the Japanese adult population hold NISA accounts and 1.6% of those eligible have iDeCo accounts. The Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF)'s rate of return is, in fact, one of the lowest in the OECD countries. By 2050, every elderly person aged 65 and over will be supported by 1.2 working age persons [35].

### 6.9 Macroeconomic Context

Japan's economy has recovered moderately, although some weakness has been seen in part. The Bank of Japan expects to achieve the price stability target of 2 percent sometime during the second half of the projection period of its latest Outlook — namely, the period from the second half of fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2027. The Bank of Japan raised its policy interest rate in June from 0.75% to 1%, and is expected to tighten policy further. The real consumer activity index was up 2.7% in May—the strongest rate of growth in more than three years [43][42].

The Bank of Japan decided to reduce the amount of its monthly outright purchases of JGBs, which had been close to 6 trillion yen, by about 400 billion yen each calendar quarter through March 2026 [42].

Japan has a highly developed market-oriented economy. Japan is the fourth-largest economy in the world by nominal GDP and the fifth-largest by purchasing power parity (PPP). Since the collapse of the Japanese asset price bubble in the early 1990s, the country has experienced a prolonged period of economic stagnation referred to as the Lost Decades. As of 2021, Japan has significantly higher public debt than other developed nations, at approximately 260% of GDP. 45% of this debt is held by the Bank of Japan, and most of the remainder is also held domestically. The Japanese economy faces considerable challenges posed by an ageing and declining population, which peaked at 128.5 million people in 2010 and has fallen to 122.6 million people in 2024 [41].

---

## 7. ACADEMIC STUDIES ON THE SILVER ECONOMY

### 7.1 Academic Paper: Japan's Aging Society: Policy, Lesson and the Silver Economy

This academic paper by Siriporn Dabphet (Srinakharinwirot University, Bangkok, Thailand) examines Japan's aging society policies, lessons learned, and the potential of the silver economy. Published in PEOPLE: International Journal of Social Sciences on July 14, 2025. The study uses documentary research to analyze Japan's demographic transition. Japan became an aging society in the 1970s and has since become the world's oldest super-aged society. The demographic shift has led to a reduced young workforce, declining personal income tax revenue, and increased government expenditure on elderly welfare. In response, Japan implemented proactive aging strategies across both public and private sectors, including public healthcare systems, medical treatment, pension insurance, and home care services. The growing elderly population is reshaping Japan's economy and consumption patterns, with both government and private businesses developing products, innovations, and services tailored to elderly individuals—collectively known as the silver economy. The paper suggests that other countries can benefit from studying Japan's experience with an aging society [1].

### 7.2 Academic Paper: The Silver-Hair Economy in the New Era: Political Economy Perspectives

This academic article published in *Sustainability* (2025, Vol. 17, Issue 15, 6760) by Li, Xie, Luo, and Yang from the National University of Defense Technology, China. The article analyzes the silver economy through the lens of Marxist political economy, examining surplus value, labor markets, and capital dynamics. The authors propose a novel "Political Economy—Multiple Streams Intersection Model" combining Marxist theory with Kingdon's Multiple Streams Theory to analyze policy processes. Key findings include: China's population aged 65+ grew from 98 million (7.58%) in 2004 to 217 million (15.40%) in 2023, transitioning to moderate aging in just 20 years versus 45+ years typically for developed countries. The silver economy is defined as 'all economic activities driven by public and consumer expenditures related to the population aged over 50' [4].

### 7.3 Academic Paper: The Co-Evolution of Markets and Regulation in the Japanese Functional Food Industry

This peer-reviewed academic article by Sato, Kodama, and Sengoku (2025) published in Foods. The study examines the historical evolution of Japan's functional food regulations from the 1960s, proposing a risk-side/benefit-side framework. Key findings: Japan's multi-tiered regulatory system includes FOSHU, FNFC, and FFC, plus unregulated "so-called health foods." The FFC system (introduced in 2015) uses a notification-based approach, leading to rapid market expansion from JPY 31 billion to JPY 357 billion by 2020, surpassing FOSHU. The Beni-koji (red yeast rice) contamination incident in 2024 highlighted regulatory adjustments needed. Globally, the functional food market is a substantial and rapidly expanding segment, valued at nearly USD five hundred billion and consistently projected to grow at high double-digit compound annual growth rates (CAGRs) [15].

### 7.4 Academic Paper: The Process of Urban Older People Surrendering Their Driver's License

Published in Sage Open Aging on July 1, 2025 (PMCID: PMC12219472). Conducted by researchers from Tokyo University of Technology, Juntendo University Hospital, and Sendai Seiyo Gakuin Collage. Used the Trajectory Equifinality Model (TEM) with semi-structured interviews of four participants (aged 75–82, mean 77.3 years). Four phases identified: Driving Continuation Phase, Driving Cessation Preparation Phase, Lifestyle Confidence Phase, and License Surrender Decision Phase. Key finding: distinction between practical driving cessation and formal license surrender, which do not always coincide [24].

### 7.5 Academic Paper: Adapting to new mobility conditions (Travel Behaviour and Society)

Published in Travel Behaviour and Society (Volume 43, April 2026). Examined how people in Shiga prefecture, Japan, might substitute in-person mobility with online services for daily necessities if their driver's licenses were revoked. Used a stated-choice survey of 645 individuals. Found that older adults are generally willing to shift from car use to public transport rather than forgo travel entirely. In-person activities are less replaceable for older adults, likely due to the sensory nature of shopping and the relational quality of social interaction [25].

### 7.6 Academic Paper: Household energy consumption pattern changes in an aging society

Published in PubMed (PMC8530012). Examines how population aging affects household energy consumption in Japan using micro-level data from 1989 to 2014. Assesses three effects: pure aging effect, cohort effect, and family structure effect. Found that household energy consumption increased by about 12% from 1995 to 2015 due to aging. Household energy consumption increased by about 16.6% from 1990 to 2015 due to shrinking household size. The cohort born 1975-1980 uses 16.7% less energy than those born 1950-1954 [29].

### 7.7 Academic Paper: Increasing single households challenges household decarbonization in Japan

Published in *Global Environmental Change* (Volume 86, May 2024) by Liqiao Huang, Yin Long, Zhiheng Chen, Yuan Li, Jiamin Ou, Yosuke Shigetomi, and Yoshikuni Yoshida. Examines how the rise of single-person households affects household carbon footprints. Found that single households present higher carbon footprints than non-single households, with single females surpassing males. By 2040, single households are expected to account for approximately 31.1% of Japan's total household emissions [30].

### 7.8 Academic Paper: Japan's Pension Reforms: Assessing Challenges

Published in Journal of Sustainable Development, Vol. 18, No. 3, 2025. Examines Japan's pension system challenges and reform proposals. Uses qualitative interpretivist approach with Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Four themes: (1) Demographic Shifts; (2) Financial Sustainability; (3) Policy Responses; (4) Societal Impacts. Compares international pension models. Proposes "Elder Eco Pension Synergy" framework. Emphasizes that Japan's collectivist culture (ringi-sei decision-making, filial piety/oyakoko) requires culturally adapted solutions [33].

### 7.9 Academic Paper: Revising nursing home design standards and regulations

Published in *Frontiers in Public Health* (2025). Proposes revisions to Japan's nursing home design standards by integrating smart devices. Three-phase methodology reviewing existing Japanese regulations (Older Population Welfare Act, Barrier-Free Law). Six demand categories: Family Care, Daily Care, Safe Mobility, Privacy, Daily Recreation, and Achieving Value. Proposes reclassifying four of six core welfare services as "smart services" enabled by IoT, AI, and remote monitoring technologies [20].

### 7.10 Academic Paper: Relationship Between Urban Environment and Changes in Health Status

A 2025 study analyzed the relationship between changes in health status and the urban/transportation environment among elderly Japanese individuals who have returned their driver's licenses. Using panel survey data from 2022 and 2023 in Funabashi City, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, the study examined 180 respondents aged 65+ who had returned their licenses. The results showed that the more facilities around the home, such as supermarkets, the less the decline in activity capacity [22].

### 7.11 Silver Economy Market Size Estimates

**Global Silver Economy Market:**
- Valued at USD 3,028,023.44 million in 2025, projected to reach USD 5,398,937.97 million by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 7.5% [2].
- Telehealth/remote-care usage among seniors rose 44%, with over 520 million seniors accessing digital health platforms across 72 countries [2].
- Smart-home assistive installations increased 27% in senior households [2].
- Demand for age-friendly mobility devices and ergonomic furniture grew 33% (over 14 million units sold globally in 2024) [2].
- About 38% of seniors globally reported limited access to age-friendly accommodations or transport systems [2].

**Silver Economy Market (Alternative Estimate):**
- Valued at $17.8 billion in 2025, projected to reach $34.6 billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 7.7% [3].
- Asia Pacific: 36.2% share ($6.4B) — highest CAGR at 8.6%, led by Japan, China, South Korea [3].
- Healthcare segment: 38.4% share ($6.8B) — largest, CAGR 8.1% [3].
- The 60-70 years age group dominates with 45.8% share ($8.1B) [3].

**Japan Silver Economy:**
- The silver economy is projected to reach ¥100 trillion by 2030 (Cabinet Office Japan projection) [5].
- Japan has 125 million people, of whom 30% are over 65. That is not primarily a problem. It is the largest concentration of predictable, inelastic, high-purchasing-power demand on the planet [5].
- Japanese consumers in the eldercare and health categories pay quality premiums of 30–60% over comparable Western markets [5].

### 7.12 Employment Among Seniors

Nearly 6.1 million people aged 65 and over are currently employed in Japan [7].

By 2030, those over 50 will constitute 32% of the Asia-Pacific population, but are expected to contribute 52% of the total Asia-Pacific consumer expenditure. Smartphone penetration for 50+ grows at 22% annually (2.4x faster than 18-34) [7].

### 7.13 Key Consulting Firm Insights

**McKinsey**: Japan faces a labor-market gap; nearly 6.1 million aged 65+ are employed. Businesses should develop senior-focused products (e.g., Tokutake's Ayumi shoes, Benry Corporation's delivery services), promote youthfulness (e.g., Curves International fitness for women 50+), and ease isolation (e.g., Kozocom's Kozo SNS Village for ages 50+) [7].

**Deloitte ("The Silver Avalanche")**: By 2030, those over 50 will constitute 32% of Asia-Pacific population but contribute 52% of consumer expenditure. Smartphone penetration for 50+ grows at 22% annually (2.4x faster than 18-34). Key sector opportunities: healthcare/wellness (integrated health platforms), financial services (senior-friendly mobile banking), travel/leisure (barrier-free tour packages, Expo 2025 Osaka), and housing (retirement communities, home modification) [7].

**EY ("Well-Being Technology")**: Focuses on four elements: mental health (biometric monitoring), physical health (fitness tracking, VR/AR rehab, telehealth), social well-being (digital community platforms), and financial security (AI-driven robo-advisors). Benefits include enhanced health monitoring, caregiver support, and improved accessibility. Challenges include digital literacy, privacy/data security, and need for support systems [7].

### 7.14 OECD Economic Survey: Japan 2026

The OECD Economic Survey for Japan 2026 discusses key policy insights for Japan's economy in the context of an aging society [40].

The average normal retirement age among OECD countries will increase from 64.7 and 63.9 years for men and women retiring in 2024 to 66.4 and 65.9 years, respectively, when starting the career in 2024 [39]. On average across OECD countries, full-career average-wage workers entering the labour market now will receive a net pension at 63% of net wages. For low earners (half average wage), the rate is 76% [39].

--- SOURCE 13: Is Aging Behind Japan’s Drop in Consumer Spending? ---
URL: https://richardkatz.substack.com/p/is-aging-behind-japans-drop-in-consumer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from Richard Katz's 'Japan Economy Watch' (published around December 2023) examines whether Japan's aging population is the primary driver of the decade-long decline in consumer spending. While consumer spending is down 3% from 2013 levels (despite GDP rising 5%), and the share of senior-led households (65+) rose from 38% (2012) to 45% (2022), the author argues aging is NOT the cause. The key insight is a per capita vs. per household distinction: senior households have fewer people (1.87 vs. 2.55), so seniors actually spend about 7% more per person than younger households. Seniors spend more per person on basics like housing (22% vs. 20%), food (28% vs. 24%), and out-of-pocket healthcare (6% vs. 4%), partly due to economies of scale. Overall, consumption per capita fell only 1.3% from 2012-2022. The author concludes the drop in consumption is due to a ~2% population decline since 2013 and stagnant/falling income, not aging.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Older people spend less, he contended. Intuitively, that sounded right, so I looked it up. It turns out not to be true.","On average, under-60 households have 2.55 persons per household, whereas senior households have just 1.87. As a result, seniors actually spend about 7% more per person.","Seniors spend much more than younger households on inviting friends over for dinner, about the same on culture and recreation, and far less on educational expenses.","The bottom line: aging is not the cause of falling consumption. Part is due to an almost 2% decline in the number of people since 2013 and part is due to stagnant and/or falling income."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Japan Center for Economic Research (JCER) published a column by Senior Research Fellow Jun Saito on December 18, 2025, analyzing how Japanese households are coping with persistent price increases. The CPI rose 3.0% year-over-year in October 2025, still above the Bank of Japan's 2% target. Food prices increased 7.1% and fuel/light/water charges rose 4.3%, outpacing the overall CPI of 3.9%.

Households increased total consumption expenditure by 7.4% in nominal terms, with transportation and communication (15.7%) showing the highest growth. However, when analyzing data by annual income deciles, stark differences emerge. The first (lowest) decile households experienced a 2.2% decline in total income, forcing them to cut spending on both necessities and non-necessities more than other groups.

Key findings:
- First decile households showed lower expenditure growth in 7 of 10 consumption subgroups compared to average households
- For necessities like food, first decile households reduced spending through substitution (e.g., buying less bread, dairy, fresh vegetables while still purchasing rice)
- Policy measures (free school meals, electricity/gas subsidies, free water basic charges in Tokyo) had differential impacts across income groups
- The first decile spent more than others on housing (higher rent burden), education (higher school fees due to abolition of income testing for tuition support), and other consumption (increased remittances to support family members)

The author concludes that policy measures to address price increases must account for income differences, as programs like energy subsidies and petrol price caps tend to disproportionately benefit higher-income households who use more energy and own more vehicles.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank (三井住友信託銀行) provides a comprehensive analysis of retirement living expenses in Japan, based on data from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' 2024 Household Survey. 

Key data points include:
- **Couple households (65+):** Average monthly living expenses of ¥286,877 (consumption ¥256,521 + non-consumption ¥30,356), with food (¥76,352), transportation/communication (¥27,768), and education/entertainment (¥25,377) as major categories.
- **Single-person households (65+):** Average monthly expenses of ¥161,933 (consumption ¥149,286 + non-consumption ¥12,647).

The article highlights that 82.2% of respondents express anxiety about retirement funds (2022 Life Security Survey by the Japan Institute of Life Insurance), and 73.9% believe pensions alone are insufficient. The minimum monthly living cost needed is ¥231,000, while a "comfortable" retirement requires ¥379,000/month—far exceeding the average pension of ¥147,000/month per person.

Beyond regular living expenses, retirees should plan for: insurance premiums, home repairs/renovations (¥1-2 million for exteriors, ¥500,000-2 million for plumbing), medical/nursing care costs (¥30,000-80,000/month for in-home care; ¥150,000-350,000/month for nursing homes), ceremonial occasions (¥50,000-150,000 per event), and support for children/grandchildren.

The article recommends preparing through: NISA (tax-free investment accounts, up to ¥3.6 million/year investment limit, ¥18 million lifetime limit), iDeCo (individual defined contribution pension plans with tax benefits), savings-type insurance, individual government bonds, foreign currency deposits, and stock investments. It emphasizes early planning, diversified asset allocation, and long-term accumulation.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The OECD Economic Survey of Japan 2024 assesses Japan's economic situation and policy challenges. Key findings include:

**Macroeconomic Outlook:** The post-pandemic recovery has recently lost momentum, with GDP growth moderating to 1.0% in 2024 and 1.1% in 2025. Inflation has risen above the 2% target since April 2022, with headline CPI at 3.2% in 2023 and projected to moderate to 2.0% in 2025. The labour market remains tight, and wage growth gained traction with the highest Shunto wage negotiations in three decades (3.6% headline increase).

**Monetary and Financial Stability:** The Bank of Japan maintains -0.1% short-term policy rate but has increased flexibility in yield curve control since December 2022. The OECD recommends further flexibility and gradual rate increases if inflation is projected to remain around 2% durably. Financial stability risks require monitoring of foreign interest rate risks, pandemic-era loan repayments, and regional bank vulnerabilities.

**Fiscal Policy:** Gross public debt reached 245% of GDP in 2022, the highest among OECD countries. The OECD recommends reducing the fiscal deficit, elaborating a credible roadmap for primary surplus, limiting supplementary budgets, and gradually increasing the consumption tax rate from the current 10%. Health and long-term care reforms are needed to contain spending growth.

**Productivity and Innovation:** SME R&D spending is low (6% of total R&D). Business dynamism is weak with few start-ups. Recommendations include making the R&D tax credit refundable, promoting venture capital, reducing government loan guarantees, and improving the innovation framework.

**Climate Change:** Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is challenging given heavy reliance on fossil fuels (renewables provide only 11% of total energy supply). The OECD recommends improving carbon pricing, enhancing electricity grid investment, and developing contingency roadmaps for uncertain technologies.

**Demographic Challenges:** Japan's fertility rate of 1.3 is among the lowest globally. The old-age dependency ratio is projected to reach 79% by 2050. The OECD recommends increasing parental leave take-up (especially for men), breaking down labour market dualism, abolishing mandatory retirement, raising the pension eligibility age, and improving integration policies for foreign workers. Past reforms under Abenomics raised growth and labour market participation, particularly of women and older workers.

| Fukuoka City | ~¥65,000 | Rising fast; 20% YoY rent increases |

**Takeaway:** ¥250k/month goes further in Osaka/Fukuoka but feels adequate in Tokyo.

## Household Type Breakdown

- **Single:** Average ¥167k/month nationally; ¥180k–¥240k in Tokyo; can go as low as ¥100k–¥150k frugally
- **Couple (no kids):** Average ~¥264,000/month total (1.5–1.6x a single, not double, due to shared expenses)
- **Family with one child:** Average ~¥312,000/month; need ¥300k–¥400k for comfortable urban living; international schools add ~¥167k+/month per child

## Major Expense Categories

**Housing (Rent):** National average ~¥59,656/month; Tokyo average ~¥87,126/month. One-time move-in costs can total 4–6 months' rent (~¥350k for an ¥80k apartment) including deposit, key money, agent fee, guarantor fee, etc.

**Utilities:** Average household: ¥23,111/month; Single: ~¥12,452/month. Electricity ~¥6,529/month for singles; Gas ¥2,000–¥3,000; Water ~¥1,500–¥2,000/month.

**Communications:** Internet ~¥4,000–¥6,000/month; Mobile phone ~¥6,802/month average (or ¥2k–¥4k with MVNOs).

**Food:** Average single: ~¥43,941/month; Average household: ~¥69,530/month. Home cooking can be ¥30k–¥40k for a single; dining out adds significantly (ramen lunch ¥700–¥1,000; dinner ¥2,000–¥3,000).

**Transportation:** Single average: ~¥12,504/month. Commuter passes ¥5k–¥15k/month. Car ownership: ¥20k–¥50k/month including parking, gas, insurance.

**Health Insurance:** Employer plans: ~5% of salary (employee share). National Health Insurance: ¥2k–¥3k/month minimum up to ¥20k+ for higher income. 70% of medical costs covered; 30% out-of-pocket.

**Taxes & Social Security:** Income tax (5%–20% progressive) + Resident tax (~10% of prior year's income, not due in first year) + Pension (¥17k/month flat for National Pension, or ~9% of salary for Employees' Pension split with employer). Total deductions can reach ~20% of gross salary.

## Foreigner-Specific Considerations

- Guarantor company fees (50–100% of one month's rent upfront)
- Premium for English-supported services
- Initial setup costs for furniture/appliances (¥100k–¥300k)
- International school tuition (¥2M+/year per child)
- No resident tax in first year (a perk)
- Visa renewal fees (~¥4,000)
- Remittance costs and exchange rate considerations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the 2025 average results summary of the Family Income and Expenditure Survey (Household Income and Expenditure Edition) published by Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (Statistics Bureau). It covers household income, expenditure, and savings for various household types.

**Key Findings for Households of Two or More Persons:**
- **Consumption expenditure** averaged 314,001 yen/month, up 4.6% nominally and 0.9% in real terms (first real increase in 3 years). The real increase was driven by rebounds in "automobile-related expenses" after the previous year's production stoppage, and increased spending on "transportation" and "recreational services" due to the Osaka-Kansai Expo.
- By category, real increases were seen in "Transportation & Communication" (+6.7%), "Education" (+6.8%), "Culture & Recreation" (+3.7%), "Housing" (+0.7%), "Fuel, Light & Water Charges" (+2.5%), and "Medical Care" (+1.9%). Real decreases were seen in "Food" (-1.2%), "Clothing & Footwear" (-1.8%), "Furniture & Household Utensils" (-0.5%), and "Other Consumption Expenditure" (-4.1%).
- The **Engel's coefficient** rose to 28.6% (up 0.3 points).
- By age group, consumption expenditure increased in real terms for all age groups except those aged 50–59.

**Key Findings for Worker Households (two or more persons):**
- **Real income** was 653,901 yen/month, up 2.8% nominally but down 0.9% in real terms.
- **Disposable income** averaged 532,408 yen, up 1.9% nominally but down 1.7% in real terms. Real decreases were seen in the 40–49 and 50–59 age groups.
- **Consumption expenditure** was 346,297 yen, up 6.5% nominally and 2.7% in real terms (real increases across all age groups).
- The **average propensity to consume** rose 2.8 points to 65.0%. The surplus (black ink) was 186,111 yen, with net financial asset increases of 194,870 yen.

**Key Findings for All Households and Single-Person Households:**
- **All households (total):** Consumption expenditure was 259,880 yen, up 3.6% nominally but down 0.1% in real terms (third consecutive year of real decline).
- **Single-person households:** Consumption expenditure was 173,042 yen, up 2.1% nominally but down 1.5% in real terms (third consecutive year of real decline).

**Key Findings for Elderly Households (65+):**
- Among elderly (65+) unemployed households of two or more persons, average consumption exceeded disposable income, resulting in a deficit (negative savings).
- **Elderly couple (both 65+, unemployed):** Average propensity to consume was 119.2%, with expenditure exceeding income.
- **Elderly single-person (65+, unemployed):** Average propensity to consume was 125.3%, also in deficit.

**Notable 2025 Events:**
- Spring labor negotiations resulted in a 5.39% wage increase (second largest since 1976).
- Summer and winter bonuses reached record highs for large corporations.
- The Osaka-Kansai Expo opened (April–October), attracting approximately 25.58 million visitors.
- The minimum wage was raised by a record 66 yen to 1,121 yen (national average).
- The gasoline temporary tax rate was abolished in December.
- The Nikkei Stock Average hit a record high of 52,411 yen on October 31.
- A record 42.68 million foreign visitors came to Japan in 2025.

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. Search: "Japan Statistics Bureau Family Income and Expenditure Survey elderly households 65+ consumption expenditure 2020-2024"

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## 1. OVERVIEW: ELDERLY HOUSEHOLD CONSUMPTION IN JAPAN

### 1.1 Definition of "Elderly Households" in Official Statistics

According to the Statistics Bureau of Japan's Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES / 家計調査), "aged households" (senior households) are defined as: (1) one-person households comprising persons aged 65 years and over; and (2) households consisting of only males aged 65 years and over and/or females aged 60 years and over, and one of household members aged 65 years and over [Source: Statista, citing FIES definition].

### 1.2 Macroeconomic Significance of Elderly Consumption

Senior consumption, defined as the consumption of households where the head of the household is aged 60 or older, was estimated at ¥115 trillion in 2014. This is 48% of overall personal consumption and corresponds to 24% of nominal GDP [Source: Nippon.com, citing Consumption Patterns of Japan's Elderly article]. The consumption expenditures of households of people aged 60 and older have grown by an annual average of 3.1% between 2003 and 2014, while consumption by households under 60 declined by 1.9% annually over the same period [Source: Nippon.com].

### 1.3 Per-Household vs. Per-Capita Spending Patterns

On a per-household basis, younger households (under 60) still spend more (¥275,000/month) than elderly households (60+) (¥230,000/month) [Source: Nippon.com]. However, according to Richard Katz's analysis of FIES data, "older people spend less... It turns out not to be true" when examined on a per-capita basis. "On average, under-60 households have 2.55 persons per household, whereas senior households have just 1.87. As a result, seniors actually spend about 7% more per person" [Source: Richard Katz, Japan Economy Watch]. Seniors spend more per person on basics like housing (22% vs. 20%), food (28% vs. 24%), and out-of-pocket healthcare (6% vs. 4%), partly due to economies of scale [Source: Richard Katz].

### 1.4 Overall Spending Levels for Elderly Households

**2024 FIES Data (as cited by Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank):**
- **Elderly (65+) couple households (unemployed):** Average monthly consumption expenditure of ¥256,521; total living expenses including non-consumption (taxes, social insurance) of ¥286,877/month [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing 2024 FIES].
- **Elderly (65+) single-person households (unemployed):** Average monthly consumption expenditure of ¥149,286; total including non-consumption of ¥161,933/month [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing 2024 FIES].

**2025 FIES Data (as cited by Japan Life Insurance Culture Center):**
- **Elderly couple (both 65+, unemployed):** Monthly disposable income of approximately ¥222,000 versus consumer spending of approximately ¥264,000, resulting in a monthly shortfall of about ¥42,000 [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].
- **Elderly single (65+, unemployed):** Monthly disposable income of approximately ¥118,000 versus consumer spending of approximately ¥148,000, resulting in a monthly shortfall of about ¥30,000 [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].

**2025 FIES Summary (from the official Statistics Bureau PDF):**
- Among elderly (65+) unemployed households of two or more persons, average consumption exceeded disposable income, resulting in a deficit (negative savings) [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- **Elderly couple (both 65+, unemployed):** Average propensity to consume was 119.2%, with expenditure exceeding income [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- **Elderly single-person (65+, unemployed):** Average propensity to consume was 125.3%, also in deficit [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].

**BigGo Finance analysis of 2024 FIES data:**
- Elderly (65+) unemployed couple households face a persistent average monthly deficit of ¥34,058 (~$215), with pension income of ~¥225,182 falling short of living expenses of ~¥256,521 [Source: BigGo Finance, citing 2024 FIES].
- Among households composed solely of individuals aged 65 and over, 55.8% felt their life was either "very difficult" or "somewhat difficult" [Source: BigGo Finance].
- The average savings for households with two or more persons where the head is aged 65 or over and unemployed reaches 25.6 million yen (approx. $161,500) [Source: BigGo Finance].
- There is a stark pension disparity: National Pension averages ¥59,310/month vs. Employees' Pension at ¥150,289/month [Source: BigGo Finance].

---

## 2. EXPENDITURE BY CATEGORY FOR ELDERLY HOUSEHOLDS

### 2.1 Food (食料)

Food is the largest consumption expenditure category for the elderly [Source: Nippon.com]. Elderly households show preferences for fresh fish, vegetables, and fruits over eating out [Source: Nippon.com].

**Specific data points:**
- For elderly (65+) unemployed couple households (2024 FIES): Food expenditure of **¥76,352/month** [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing 2024 FIES].
- Per Richard Katz's analysis, seniors spend about 28% of their consumption budget on food, compared to 24% for younger households [Source: Richard Katz].
- For reference (all 2+ person households, 2025 FIES): Food expenditure was a major component with national 2+ person household Engel coefficient at 28.6% (up 0.3 points) [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- For 2025, real food expenditure for 2+ person households declined by 1.2% in real terms [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- Single-person household (2025): Food expenditure approximately ¥45,800/month [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].
- Two-or-more-person household (2025): Food expenditure approximately ¥93,800/month [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].
- National average 1-person household (2025): Food ¥49,320/month [Source: Japan Dev, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications data].
- The Japan Center for Economic Research reported that food prices increased 7.1% year-over-year as of October 2025, outpacing the overall CPI of 3.9% [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].

### 2.2 Clothing and Footwear (被服及び履物)

Elderly households have lower spending on clothing compared to younger households [Source: Nippon.com].

**Specific data points:**
- For 2025, real clothing and footwear expenditure for 2+ person households declined by 1.8% in real terms [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- National average 1-person household (2025): Clothing & footwear ¥4,908/month [Source: Japan Dev, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications data].
- In June 2026, overall household spending on clothing declined 19.9% year-over-year [Source: Trading Economics, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs & Communications].
- For the "age of household head 70+" group (2+ person households), total monthly consumption was approximately ¥253,000, with clothing being a relatively small share [Source: Habitto, citing 2024-2025 FIES].

### 2.3 Housing (住居)

Housing includes rent, repairs, maintenance, and imputed rent. Elderly households have lower spending on housing compared to younger households on a per-household basis, but higher on a per-person basis [Source: Nippon.com; Richard Katz].

**Specific data points:**
- Per Richard Katz's analysis, seniors spend about 22% of their consumption budget on housing, compared to 20% for younger households (on a per-person basis) [Source: Richard Katz].
- For 2025, real housing expenditure for 2+ person households increased by 0.7% in real terms [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- National average 1-person household (2025): Housing ¥21,666/month (note: 60.1% of single-person households are homeowners, bringing averages down) [Source: Japan Dev, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications].
- Single-person household (2025): Housing approximately ¥30,300/month [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].
- For reference, the first (lowest income) decile households spent more than others on housing (higher rent burden) according to JCER analysis [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- National average rent for a single person: ~¥59,656/month; Tokyo average: ~¥87,126/month [Source: E-Housing, citing 2024 data].

### 2.4 Transportation (交通)

Transportation includes public transport, vehicle purchase/maintenance, and fuel. Elderly households have lower spending on transportation compared to younger households [Source: Nippon.com].

**Specific data points:**
- For elderly (65+) unemployed couple households (2024 FIES): Transportation and communication combined expenditure of **¥27,768/month** [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing 2024 FIES].
- For 2025, transportation & communication for 2+ person households increased by 6.7% in real terms (the highest increase among all categories). This was driven by rebounds in "automobile-related expenses" after the previous year's production stoppage, and increased spending on "transportation" due to the Osaka-Kansai Expo [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- Two-or-more-person household (2025): Transportation/Communication approximately ¥56,900/month [Source: Japan Life Insurance Culture Center, citing 2025 FIES].
- National average 1-person household (2025): Transportation & communication ¥19,333/month [Source: Japan Dev, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications].
- Single-person average: Transportation ~¥12,504/month [Source: E-Housing].
- In June 2026, overall household spending on transport declined 5.7% year-over-year [Source: Trading Economics, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs & Communications].
- The JCER noted that transportation and communication showed the highest nominal growth (15.7%) among all consumption categories as of October 2025, driven by price increases and vehicle purchases [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- The gasoline temporary tax rate was abolished in December 2025, which may affect transportation costs going forward [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].

---

## 3. AGE SUBGROUP ANALYSIS: YOUNGER ELDERLY (65-74) VS. OLDER ELDERLY (75+)

### 3.1 Total Consumption by Age of Household Head

Based on the FIES data for 2+ person households by age of household head:

- **Under 40:** ~¥280,000/month (high housing costs)
- **40-49:** ~¥331,000/month (education costs increasing)
- **50-59:** ~¥357,000/month (peak spending, children's university)
- **60-69:** ~¥311,000/month (post-retirement)
- **70+:** ~¥253,000/month (medical costs increase)

[Source: Habitto, citing 2024-2025 FIES]

### 3.2 Propensity to Consume by Age

The 2025 FIES Summary reports that by age group, consumption expenditure increased in real terms for all age groups except those aged 50–59 [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].

### 3.3 Income Constraints by Age

54% of people aged 70 and older have annual incomes less than ¥2 million. The number of households headed by people aged 70 and older with total annual incomes less than ¥2 million has grown 1.4 times to 450,000 from 320,000 five years ago and 2.2 times from 200,000 ten years ago [Source: Nippon.com].

---

## 4. TREND DATA: CHANGES OVER THE PAST DECADE

### 4.1 Long-Term Growth Trends

- Consumption by elderly households (60+) grew at an annual average of 3.1% between 2003-2014, while consumption by households under 60 declined by 1.9% annually over the same period [Source: Nippon.com].
- The elderly population is projected to grow by only 0.4% annually from 2017-2025, while the working-age population (20-59) is contracting rapidly [Source: Nippon.com].

### 4.2 Recent Year-over-Year Changes (2024-2025)

**2025 Annual Results (2+ person households):**
- Total consumption: 314,001 yen/month, up 4.6% nominally and 0.9% in real terms (first real increase in 3 years) [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].
- Real increases: Transportation & Communication (+6.7%), Housing (+0.7%), Fuel, Light & Water Charges (+2.5%), Medical Care (+1.9%)
- Real decreases: Food (-1.2%), Clothing & Footwear (-1.8%)
- The Engel coefficient rose to 28.6% (up 0.3 points) [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, 2025 FIES Summary].

**2024 Annual Results:**
- For 2+ person households in 2024, average monthly consumption spending was 300,243 yen [Source: Habitto, citing 2024 FIES; Statistics Bureau of Japan].
- December 2024 household spending rose 2.7% year-on-year in real terms, beating expectations of 0.2% rise, marking its first increase since July 2024. Average household expenditure stood at 352,633 yen ($2,332) [Source: CNBC, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs & Communications].

### 4.3 2026 Data (Most Recent)

- June 2026: For 2+ person households, average monthly consumption expenditures were 290,886 yen, down 1.5% in nominal terms and down 3.3% in real terms year-over-year [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, June 2026 FIES].
- June 2026: Household spending dropped 3.3% year-on-year, the seventh consecutive month of contraction and the sharpest drop in the sequence. Spending declined across food (-2.5%), utilities (-7.1%), furniture (-11.4%), clothing (-19.9%), and transport (-5.7%) [Source: Trading Economics, citing Ministry of Internal Affairs & Communications].
- The average of monthly income per household for workers' households stood at 1,013,986 yen in June 2026, up 3.9% in nominal terms and up 2.0% in real terms from the previous year [Source: Statistics Bureau of Japan, June 2026 FIES].

### 4.4 Inflation Impact on Categories

- CPI rose 3.0% year-over-year in October 2025, still above the Bank of Japan's 2% target [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- Food prices increased 7.1% and fuel/light/water charges rose 4.3%, outpacing the overall CPI of 3.9% (excluding imputed rent) [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- Households increased total consumption expenditure by 7.4% in nominal terms, with transportation and communication (15.7%) showing the highest growth [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- The first (lowest income) decile households experienced a 2.2% decline in total income, forcing them to cut spending on both necessities and non-necessities [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- First decile households reduced spending through substitution (e.g., buying less bread, dairy, fresh vegetables while still purchasing rice) [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].
- First decile spent more than others on housing (higher rent burden) [Source: JCER, Dec 2025].

## 6. KEY STRUCTURAL CHARACTERISTICS OF ELDERLY SPENDING

### 6.1 Deficit Spending and Savings Drawdown

Elderly households in Japan consistently run monthly deficits. Elderly (65+) unemployed couple households face a persistent average monthly deficit of ¥34,058 (~$215), with pension income of ~¥225,182 falling short of living expenses of ~¥256,521. The shortfall is covered by drawing down savings, which average 25.6 million yen (up from 22.18 million in 2019). Asset composition is shifting from deposits toward securities (now 19.6% of holdings) [Source: BigGo Finance, citing 2024 FIES].

### 6.2 Category-Specific Patterns for Elderly

- **Food:** Largest expenditure category; preferences for fresh fish, vegetables, and fruits over eating out [Source: Nippon.com].
- **Housing:** Lower spending than younger households in absolute terms but higher per person [Source: Nippon.com; Richard Katz].
- **Clothing:** Lower spending than younger households [Source: Nippon.com].
- **Transportation:** Lower spending than younger households [Source: Nippon.com].
- **Medical Care:** High medical care expenses [Source: Nippon.com].
- **Social Expenses:** High spending on gifts and dining out [Source: Nippon.com].

### 6.3 Income Constraints

The average pension amount is approximately ¥147,000/month per person for Employees' Pension recipients. For those receiving only the National Pension, the average is ¥59,310/month [Source: BigGo Finance; Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank]. 82.2% of respondents express anxiety about retirement funds, and 73.9% believe pensions alone are insufficient [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing 2022 Life Security Survey]. The minimum monthly living cost needed for retirement is ¥231,000, while a "comfortable" retirement requires ¥379,000/month [Source: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, citing Japan Life Insurance Culture Center survey].

--- SOURCE 10: 新・将来推計人口がまさかの上方修正に ～楽観的だと考える２つの理由～ | 星野 卓也 | 第一ライフ資産運用経済研究所 ---
URL: https://www.dlri.co.jp/report/macro/247038.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report by economist Takuya Hoshino (First Life Group Economic Research Institute) analyzes the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research's 2023 revision of Japan's future population projections, published April 27, 2023.

**Key Findings:**
- Surprisingly, Japan's total population projection for 2065 was revised UPWARD from 88.08 million (2017 projection) to 91.59 million (2023 projection), despite birth rates falling faster than previously assumed.
- The upward revision is primarily due to a significant increase in foreign immigration assumptions. The 2023 projection assumes foreign inflows at 2016-2019 average levels, which were much higher than previous estimates.
- Foreigners' share of total population is projected to nearly double: 4.7% (2017 projection) → 9.8% (2023 projection) by 2065, reaching 10.8% by 2070.
- Working-age population (15-64) ratio has been revised upward, while elderly and child dependency ratios were revised downward, improving labor force and social security outlooks.

**Two Reasons the Author Considers the Projection Too Optimistic:**
1. As wages in developing countries catch up to Japan's, the attractiveness of working in Japan may decline, reducing future foreign labor inflows.
2. The projection assumes the recent birth rate decline is a temporary COVID-19 effect, but the decline actually began in 2019 (pre-COVID), suggesting structural factors may keep birth rates low.

**Policy Implications:**
These population projections feed into the Cabinet Office's medium-to-long-term economic projections (affecting potential growth rate calculations) and the pension system's financial verification (affecting income replacement rate projections). The upward revision of working-age population and improved demographic balance will likely have positive effects on these simulations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

**History & Name Origin:**
The city's name comes from combining characters from the neighboring stations "Kokubunji" (国分寺) and "Tachikawa" (立川) — hence "Kunitachi" (国立). The area was originally Yabo Village (谷保村). In 1926, the Hakone Land Company (now Seibu Group) developed the area as a "university town" modeled after Göttingen, Germany, centered around Hitotsubashi University, which relocated there in 1927. Kunitachi gained town status in 1951 and city status on January 1, 1967.

**Cultural & Educational Character:**
Kunitachi is known as a "cultural and educational city" (文教都市). In 1952, it became the first area in Tokyo designated as a "cultural and educational district," restricting entertainment businesses like pachinko parlors and adult establishments. This was driven by citizens and students concerned about moral decay during the Korean War era due to the nearby US military base in Tachikawa.

**Key Features:**
- The "University Avenue" (大学通り) lined with cherry blossom and ginkgo trees runs from Kunitachi Station to Yabo Station
- Home to Hitotsubashi University, Tokyo Women's College of Physical Education, and several other educational institutions
- The old Kunitachi Station building (with its iconic triangular roof) was dismantled in 2008 but reconstructed in 2020 as a meeting place and exhibition space
- Landmark: Yabo Tenmangu Shrine, Kanematsu Hall at Hitotsubashi University (Registered Tangible Cultural Property)

**Government:**
Current mayor: Shinya Hamasaki (濵﨑真也), term starting December 25, 2024. The city was notable for disconnecting from the Basic Resident Registration Network (Juki Net) in 2002 over privacy concerns, but reconnected in 2012 after a court ruling.

**Notable Foods:**
Claimed as the birthplace of "Stamina Don" (sutadon) and "Abura Soba" (oil noodles). Also produces local wine, sake, spinach udon, and fair trade chocolate.

**Transportation:**
JR East: Chuo Line (Kunitachi Station), Nambu Line (Yabo Station, Yagawa Station). Central Expressway (Kunitachi-Fuchu IC). National Route 20 (Koshu Kaido/Hino Bypass).

**Key findings:**

- **Aging population:** Japan's aging rate has risen rapidly from 12.1% (1990) to 28.6% (2020), and is projected to reach 37.1% by 2050. While no prefectures had an aging rate over 40% in 2020, 25 prefectures are expected to exceed that threshold by 2050.

**Key concerns:**

1. **Declining living convenience:** Essential services (hospitals, elderly care facilities) have less than 50% probability of being located in towns with populations under 10,000. This creates a negative cycle of service withdrawal, out-migration, and further decline.

2. **Public transportation decline:** Both railways and buses are seeing declining passenger numbers (not yet recovered from COVID-19), with approximately 90% of operators running deficits. The elderly are most affected, citing reduced mobility for shopping and medical visits.

3. **Infrastructure aging:** Much of Japan's infrastructure was built during the high-growth period and is rapidly aging. Over 80% of survey respondents consider addressing infrastructure aging important.
